**HYPOTHESIS**

For black respondents in the NLSY79 cohort, incarceration — any residence in a jail/facility between 1985 and 1994, recorded as a binary indicator with no duration or timing granularity — is associated with substantially lower wealth by 1990 and especially 1996, and the penalty grows with baseline economic status. Because the dataset contains no income variable, "income level" is proxied by 1985 composite wealth (baseline wealth level), binned into four groups; the finding is about early economic status, not measured income. Among the 159 jailed black respondents (5.3% of 3,013), mean composite wealth was $10,393 in 1996 versus $48,865 for the non-jailed (mean gap ≈ −$38,500; median $0 vs $5,000), and only 35% of jailed respondents held positive wealth in 1996 vs 62% of non-jailed. The gap widens over time: ≈ −$5,000 in 1985 → −$12,400 in 1990 → −$38,500 in 1996 (mean, jailed minus non-jailed). By baseline wealth bin, the 1996 mean gap is ≈ −$17k (≤$0), −$34k ($1–5k), −$69k ($5–20k), and −$76k (>$20k) — negative in all four bins and largest in absolute dollars among those starting wealthiest; 1990 gaps are negative in three of four bins (the $5–20k bin's mean gap is slightly positive at +$9.5k with n=28 jailed, but its median gap is −$9.5k). Supplementary OLS (robust SEs, controlling for baseline bin and sex) gives a jailed coefficient of −$38,100 (p<0.001) on 1996 wealth, stable in sign across winsorized (−$28,800) and black-male-only (−$39,000) specifications; the jailed × baseline-bin interaction is negative in all four bins (−$20k to −$59k, significant in three) but imprecise in the >$20k cell (n=11 jailed), so the descriptive per-bin gaps are the primary evidence. Caveat: income is unobserved and proxied by baseline wealth, and 1985 wealth is concurrent with the start of the 1985–1994 jail window (jailed blacks already averaged ≈$5,000 less in 1985), so part of the gap reflects pre-incarceration disadvantage rather than a causal effect of incarceration.
